utterances.text: I apologise again, Your Honour, but we understand that the position from which the picture was taken is different from the position which Mr. Hutsch claims to have been and which he referred to as observation point number 1. He was asked questions, I think, by the Prosecutor and by both Defence in relation to that matter, and also it is the evidence of Mr. Hutsch himself that he could not see what was going on in the village, which explained why he moved to the other position.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well, I believe the evidence of Mr. Hutsch was that he could not see what was going on in part of the village, Your Honour. As he has just explained, he could see the eastern part of the village.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Continue, please, Mr. Saxon, and see if there's any further clarity.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Just for clarity, if I understood your evidence, from your first observation point, you could not see the western part of the village of Ljuboten. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Because your view of the western part of the village of Ljuboten was blocked by hill 631?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: But you were able to see the eastern part of the village. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Today, you described how you drove along farmers' paths to get from observation point 1 to observation point 2. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And, in your testimony today, you used the word "paths" in the plural sense.

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Just taking a look at this photograph, please, were you able to go in a straight line from observation point 1 to observation point 2, across the fields?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That was impossible, and that's what I replied truthfully.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. Can you explain then, roughly, how -- how you travelled. If it wasn't in a straight line, just roughly, what did you have to do to make it across to where observation point 2 is?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had to take several paths going to the right and to the left to get to the point, which I have marked there more or less with the "X" and with the arrow number "1," approximately.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you for that. I'd like to turn to a different topic now briefly. At page 6255 of the transcript, you explained to Mr. Mettraux that the information that you recorded at Ljuboten was combined in reporter's -- in your reporter's notebook and on maps. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can we show the witness, please, what is Exhibit P314. I was actually looking for the final image, which looks like this of Mr. Hutsch's sketches drawn onto a -- a map. I believe that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Hutsch, just very briefly, you testified, previously, this is -- this is a map which you made markings on, I believe, after 10.28 in the morning, according to your testimony, on Sunday, the 12th of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Maybe if we could zoom in a little bit on the centre of the map where Mr. Hutsch's black writing is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: You see, Mr. Hutsch, here there are a number of bits of data, including, we see, different numbers. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] I see 0607, 0838, I see 0744, I see 1048, I see 1220, and I see 1238. Can you tell us what these numbers refers to, please?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: They are the -- they are the times that I wrote down when I made my observations; for example, the shelling that I observed or the noises I heard of the explosions, the explosions of firing.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And, on the right-hand side, we see some red arrows going from the right side of the map towards the centre. What do those red arrows indicate, please?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are reconnaissance troops of the NLA, which from 1400 hours, according to unconfirmed reservations, advanced in that direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: So, in order to view the totality of the information that you recorded on the 12th of August, you would have to look at this map and your reporter's notebooks?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I would. In particular, because you can also see on this sketch on the right side, on the right of the arrows, you can see the position of a NLA company marked. Above the upper arrow, you can see a mortar position of the NLA, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Hutsch, at pages 6246 to 6248 of the transcript, Mr. Mettraux was discussing with you how you did or did not get information from the Ministry of Interior back in August of 2001. My colleague discussed with you the statement of a woman named at that time Tatiana Najdovska-Trajkovska.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If we can show the witness, please, actually we don't need to show this exhibit. If I can just say that the record indicates, the transcript, that, in one part of Ms. Najdovska-Trajkovska's statement, she said that she was not contacted by any journalists on the 10, 11, 12 of August, and she also said in her statement: "The practice of the Ministry of Interior was not to publish information on ongoing operations, information was released after the completion of operations." Do you remember this exchange?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can we play for Mr. Hutsch what is Exhibit P401, please, which is a video from early June 2001. [Videotape played].

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can we stop there, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Did you read what Mr. Boskoski was telling the media there?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well, would you agree that then, at least during this -- during this particular operation, Minister Boskoski himself gave information about the operation to the media?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can we show what is Exhibit P276, please. This is a video taken in September of 2001. It is -- the Ministry of the Interior was planning on returning its units to areas previously under the control of the NLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can we stop there, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Hutsch, did you see the journalists or members of the media sitting around a large room, previous, before we stopped here?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't really playing attention in detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can we start -- can we start again, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Stop there, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Hutsch, did you ever attend press conferences at the Ministry of Interior in a room like this?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can we move forward, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can we stop there, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Hutsch, if you have been following this, you'll see that the journalist and now police general Risto Galevski is talking about plans that are going to be implemented. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Would it be fair to say, then, that, at least in September 2001, the Ministry of Interior would provide information to the public, to the media, even before operations?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Hutsch, just briefly, can you describe --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Mettraux.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Your Honour, I apologise, but this video doesn't take of any operations. I think Mr. Saxon should be quite clear the evidence on this was about the return of the police to the villages. I think Mr. Galevski testified to that after the signing of the Ohrid Agreement and pursuant to the accord which had been reached on that matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I deeply apologise if I used the term operation too broadly, Your Honours. I didn't mean it in the sense of a combat operation. I simply meant it in terms of deploying police units to particular places that had been affected by the armed conflict. May I proceed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Carry on, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Briefly, Mr. Hutsch, in August 2001, how would you and your colleagues in the media get information from the Ministry of Interior?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: By using the telephone numbers we knew, by calling, and asking questions, to get information. Journalists like Carsten Hoffman, who worked for DPA news agency and was accredited in Skopje, was sent faxes with dates of press conferences. It was a very normal manner of communication for correspondents who were accredited to that country.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. I'd like you to turn your mind, please, to the question of the crowd of civilians that you saw near the village of Radisani, or in the village of Radisani, on the 12th of August, 2001. At pages 6206 to 6210 -- by the way, I believe you used the term "some people." Mr. Mettraux used the term "crowd, "immense crowd," "great crowd," things like that. At pages 6206 to 6210 of the transcript, and pages 6270 to 6275, Mr. Mettraux and you discussed whether there was a crowd of civilians at the entrance to Radisani. I'm wondering, please -- and Mr. Mettraux asked some questions about a document that originated from the OSCE.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can we show the witness, please, what is Exhibit 1D246, and if we can go to page 21 of this document, which bears the ERN N001-5418.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: This exhibit is perhaps only part of the Rule 65 ter exhibit. It does not have 21 pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I see. Perhaps, Mr. Mettraux can direct us to the particular area where he focussed on.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: I believe we can assist by giving the exhibit number of the document in question, which is currently being verified. I believe that the original Prosecution document was Rule 65 ter 216, and the document became, or part of the document in any case became, Exhibit 1D246. It was originally Rule 65 ter 1D925 of the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. We've found it. I'm very grateful to Ms. Guduric, and if we could focus on row 23 of the bottom half of this page.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Hutsch, I would like to you lock at the language here in the two columns on the right, please. In the column, the second column from the right, it sayings: "At the entrance of Radisani near the bridge, it gives a number, "a crowd is gathered with iron pipes in their hands waiting for the refugees." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And then in the next -- the next section on the far right, it says: "Team will meet with the refugees, together with the ICRC, on their way along the river. CMC was informed about the crowd at the bridge. The latter body promised to send a police team on that particular spot." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Would you agree with me there that, in those two excerpts, it uses -- we just see the word "crowd." We don't see any estimate of numbers of people?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: It doesn't say "large crowd," does it?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: It doesn't say "great crowd," does it?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: In doesn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: "Huge crowd," do you see that?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: How about "immense crowd," do you see that?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Might I add here a word, because I wasn't able to express myself earlier. It was at 11.50 [as interpreted] that the report went into the OSCE, and --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Just one moment, please, Mr. Hutsch. Maybe there was a mistake in translation. It says 12.50 here.

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. 12.50, in Skopje, the report was received. So that would mean that the event itself would have take place two hours earlier. That what is I was trying to explain to Mr. Mettraux, but my English was not good enough to do that, obviously. The crowd of people had already dissipated at that time at 12.50, in particular because it says that at that time the police and the OSCE and the crisis management centre were trying to deal with the crisis.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. I'd like to move on to another topic, Mr. Hutsch. You were asked several questions yesterday by my learned colleague Mr. Apostolski about the man named Goran Stojkov and whether you saw Mr. Stojkov in the village of Ljuboten on the 12th of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can we show the witness, please, what is 65 ter number 2D00-676, which is Mr. Hutsch's statement from 2005, and if we could move to page 18 in the English version and page 20 in the Macedonian version. Can we please move back one page, please, and we could focus on paragraphs 131 and 132. We need to go back another page in the English version, I see, and if we can focus on paragraphs 131 and 132, please. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Hutsch, yesterday, at page 6418 of the transcript, you explained to my colleague Mr. Mettraux that: "The truth is in paragraph 131." Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Paragraph 131 starts with: "At this place, I have also seen a police officer whom I knew from before. I knew him under the name Goran. I knew him as a body-guard of Ljubco Georgievski, the former prime minister. I have seen him in this function several times." Do you see this?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And then you explain later, in that paragraph, how you learned the family name, "Stojkov," of this person. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can you explain briefly to the Judges how you learned this gentleman's last name, "Stojkov," later on?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: What happened was that my interpreter and I went to Skopje, and there we met groups of paramilitaries who belonged to the Lions, or obviously belonged to the Lions. They walked around the streets and one of them -- then I was told was Goran Stojkov, and this is where I came across the name Stojkov.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And did you recognise this person?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I then recognised him as the one from Ljuboten.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And when you saw this person and you recognised him as the person you saw in Ljuboten, and you were told this person's name was Goran Stojkov, in paragraph 131, it says, "This was in October 2001." Is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Would that be a convenient time, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We resume at 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Hutsch, at pages 6314 to 6323 of the transcript, there was a fairly long discussion between my colleague Mr. Mettraux and yourself about the bodies that you saw in the road in Ljuboten on the afternoon of the 12th of August, and whether you saw two bodies together or two bodies separate the. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can we show the witness, please, what is Exhibit P319.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: While that is coming up, yesterday you were told by my learned colleague that another Prosecution witness had said that the second body found on that road was actually 20 to 30 metres down the road from the first body, a body that you saw - well, in the photograph that we're going to see - it's on the side of the road. Mr. Hutsch, this is a photograph that you annotated during your direct examination. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And you see that, on the far right-hand side of the photograph, you drew a arrow pointing down the road. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Tell us, please, what were you trying to show by placing that arrow there?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I wanted to explain was that the second body was a little bit further away from the first body.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think we're talk being 20 to 30 metres, but again my memory might not serve me well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Do you want to try --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I see Mr. Apostolski is on his feet?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Apostolski.

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do apologise for interrupting my learned colleague, Mr. Saxon. But on page 2764 of the transcript, a detailed answer was provided to this question by the witness, so maybe my learned friend can read the answer out loud.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I'll do so, if I'm directed to, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: No. We leave the matter to you, but do bear in mind that I do not and the members of the Chamber do not at this moment remember that answer. We will undoubtedly reminded of it and will look at it in due course. There may be something you need to clarify.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I do not have my hard copy of that section of the transcript with me, but my case manager may be able to assist me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Mettraux.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: We were about to offer. We have the copy, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I would like to take my colleague's offer, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: This would be from page 2763 to 2764 of the transcript of the 27th of June of 2007. The question -- I'm sorry, the question and answer relevant to this are from line 2 to 10. It would be the second page provided to Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Lines 2 to 10 is suggested.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: On the 27th of June, Mr. Hutsch, when you drew this sketch and I asked and I said -- first, you had drawn where you saw the first body, which we see now is lying off the side of the road, and then I asked you: "Could you draw, roughly, where you saw the second body lying on the road?" Then you made some marks and you said: "So the head of this man," in other words, the second deceased, "was a little bit more there, [Indicates], to the outskirt of the blood." That was your response. Now, let me simply ask you. You've given your response to me when I asked you about the purpose of the arrow. Can you give a approximate distance of between the body that we see here in this photograph and the second body?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say, let's say, five metre, six metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: In that case, Your Honour, we will simply record that we are joining with the objection of our colleagues of the Defence of Mr. Tarculovski. The transcript revealed that the arrow at the time was to indicate that only the head was a bit further from the limit of the picture.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I don't know what the objection is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Continue, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I will do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I'd like to talk to you, Mr. Hutsch, about the hotel registry that was shown to you yesterday from the Dal Met Fu hotel it Skopje. During cross-examination yesterday, you suggested that the registry that was shown to you had been altered or falsified, and you mentioned that such things had occurred in Macedonia in the past, and you mentioned a case known as "El Masri." Can you explain to the Chamber, please, briefly, who Mr. El Masri was, what happened to him in Macedonia, and what you know about hotel records in the case of Mr. El Masri?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. El Masri is a German Lebanese citizen who, between 2002, 2003 at the end of the year, was taken to Afghanistan and -- in order to be questioned there by the American intelligence services. In the first two to three weeks, he was in the Hotel Skopski Merak in Skopje, when a investigation committee of the European Union then went to the hotel, they were introduced to a completely new set of staff; but, not only that, also the book, the registry, was presented to them, which no longer contained the name "El Masri," and they were clearly changed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And is this case known as "El Masri" is a case that is currently the subject of a investigation by members of the German parliament?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And how do you know about this case, Mr. Hutsch?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: As a -- I was working for the opposition party in this investigation committee as a member and, hence, I had access to these reports, but which have already -- which have also been discussed in a open session in the German parliament.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Moving on to another topic, Mr. Hutsch.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can we please show the witness what is Prosecution 65 ter 1030, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: This is a report from the Macedonian police, Mr. Hutsch. It was shown to you yesterday and discussed with you at pages 6262 to 6263 of the transcript. As you may recall, it describes a meeting of members of the VRMO-DPMNE Party in Cair on the 12th of August, 2001. It notes there, in the first line, that the meeting ended at 2000 hour; that is, 8.00 in the evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: My colleague is on his feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Your Honour, we would simply indicate that is not what the report says.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: My colleague is -- my colleague is correct. It does not mention the word "Cair." That is correct. I stand corrected, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: I apologise. This was not the indication that we wish to give to the Chamber. The time which is mentioned on this report does not refer to the timing of the meeting but the working hour of the person who signed this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I stand corrected.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Yesterday, you were also shown -- you were shown a statement by Prime Minister Georgievski, which I believe indicated that Mr. Boskoski arrived at this meeting at sometime around 1900 hours. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. If I remember well, then the meeting started at 7.00 p.m., and the prime minister was not quite sure whether the Minister of the Interior was -- had taken part in the meeting or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: But just to be clear, if such a meeting had taken place in the village of Cair, how long would it take to drive from Cair to the Dal Met Fu restaurant, approximately?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: A minister has special priority that is escorted by the police. I suppose that it would be ten minutes or 15 minutes maximum, in terms of duration.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. Yesterday, during cross-examination, my colleague Mr. Mettraux played you a couple of intercepts, and you talked about the fact that, on two occasions, Mr. Gezim Ostreni --

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: We would have to return to private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Private

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Hutsch, I have one more question for you, and I'd like you to answer it simply as briefly as you can, please. My colleagues have alleged that you have fabricated your evidence in this trial and that have you lied to this Tribunal. I'd like you, please, to explain to the Trial Chamber, briefly, why these allegation are true or not true.

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is no particular reason for me to have invented anything because I was not a participant in the events, and I do not intend to work in Macedonia in the future in order to gain some advantage or to suffer some disadvantage. My focus is now Iraq and Afghanistan, so that I don't really have any professional contacts with the Balkans anymore. What pains me a bit here is that last year my colleague, Huub Jaspers, and another and myself, we won a prize for European journalism, and the year before we got the second price for European investigative journalism. The commission which gave the award investigated our work thoroughly. So, in view of that, I see no reason why I would have invented anything here. It is simply the issue that Ljuboten was not important for me as a journalist. My experience from the massacre in Racak where badly researched publications caused, brought about a war. I feel that the investigations carried out in Ljuboten and how the people died and what happened in detail, to find that out would have needed a lot of resources, staffing resources, finances, et cetera. You can still see the problem in the Racak case, and that was the reason why, in this case, we decided not to continue with our research.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Hutsch, at various points in your evidence, particularly when cross-examined by Defence counsel, you were asked to identify persons who were with you as you describe certain events, or persons who told you about certain events. On each of those occasions, except one that I recall, you declined to identify the persons. I would like to point out to you, on behalf of the Chamber, that as the Chamber comes to assess your evidence, you will realise that it becomes more difficult for the Chamber to place reliance on it, and to accept it as true, when we are not in a position to know the identity of the persons you say were with you or the identity of the persons you say are the sources of your information. We would like to you take that into your consideration and to indicate whether you are prepared to revise the position that you took of not disclosing the identity of those people.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have contacted several sources and the interpreters at the time who, since the change of government in Macedonia, are afraid for their life. You know that there are protests from time to time in Macedonia, demanding for more freedom of the press, claiming that Macedonia does not reach European standards for freedom of the press; and, in view of this, as a journalist in Germany, where we enjoy a high level of freedom of press and protection of sources, which was recently confirmed by the Constitutional Court in Germany, I would not be able to carry out my duties as a journalist if I were to jeopardise my sources by revealing them. I am aware of the sources -- I will inform my sources and my companions at the time, and ask them to inform the Tribunal if they're willing to do that and contact you themselves.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Hutsch, you will realise that the Chamber has not in any way sought to compel to you disclose, but you will equally realise that it necessarily puts the acceptance of your evidence at a disadvantage when do you not disclose. So it is with that knowledge that we want to be sure that we leave this position.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Very well. You will be pleased to know, Mr. Hutsch, that that concludes your questioning. The Chamber thanks you for your two occasions when you've come to The Hague and for the time that you spent here and for the assistance that you have been able to give, and you may now, of course, leave and go about your ordinary affairs.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It's been pointed out to me that strictly we were in Private Session, and I have asked and will make an order for us to be in public session at the time when you announced the close of your re-examination and the Chamber's words to the witness, so that it will be available on the public record.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: May I make a comment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If the Chamber is so desirable, I don't see a reason why my last question to Mr. Hutsch and his response could also not be available on the public record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, we'll explore that as well. We do need to go into public session now.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, Mr. Saxon, ten minutes remain. There seems little point in moving to another witness at this point.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour. The Prosecution would then intend to continue with the direct examination of Mr. Viktor Bezruchenko starting tomorrow morning, and I have been given strict orders by my case manager to inform the Chamber and the parties that the final Macedonian translation of Exhibit P466, which is the amended expert report of Mr. Bezruchenko, has now been uploaded in e-court and is available to everyone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, if there is no other matter that can be dealt with now, we adjourn for the day, to resume tomorrow at 9.00 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Friday, the 19th day of October, 2007, at 9.00 a.m. 25
